In nineteen seventy four, psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman ran a strange experiment.
They spun a wheel that was rigged to stop at ten or sixty five.
Then they asked people what percent of African countries were in the United Nations.
People who saw ten guessed about twenty five.
People who saw sixty five guessed about forty five.
The wheel meant nothing, and still it pulled their answers a long way.
Stores use that pull every day.
A car with a high sticker price makes the discount feel generous.
A fancy dish on the menu makes the next one look fair.
Whoever names the first number sets the frame for everything after it.
To beat it, decide your own number before you look.
Write down what the item is worth to you.
Then compare real prices from three different places.
If you negotiate, say your number first.
You will drag the final price toward your side.
Follow for more ways your brain gets nudged without you noticing.

caption.en: Anchoring is the quiet trick that makes the first price you see feel normal, and a famous wheel of fortune experiment proves it.

title.en: The shelf at your kid's eye level

en.text: The best shelf spot is not at your eye level.
Walk down the cereal aisle with a child, and watch the boxes.
The sugary ones are often lower down.
Marketers know that children ask, and tired parents often give in.
The trade even has a name for it: pester power.
Shelf space is also something food companies can pay for, and pay a lot.
These payments are called slotting fees, and the Federal Trade Commission has studied them.
The best spots can go to whoever pays the store, not whoever is cheapest for you.
So the box in front of you is not always the best deal.
Look at the top shelf and the bottom shelf instead.
Compare the price per ounce, not the price of the box.
Tell your kids the rule before you even enter the store.
Let them choose one treat, and put it on the list.
A clear plan turns begging into a small game they can win.
You keep the budget, and they keep a say.
Follow if you want to shop smarter than the shelf expects.

caption.en: The cereal your child begs for sits low on purpose, and here is how supermarket shelf placement works and how to shop smarter.

en.text: Only two left in stock may mean nothing at all.
In nineteen seventy five, psychologist Stephen Worchel ran a cookie experiment.
People tasted cookies from a jar with ten, or a jar with two.
They liked the cookies from the almost empty jar more.
Same cookie, but fewer of them.
When something looks rare, your brain assumes it must be good.
Travel sites use that all the time.
In twenty nineteen, a British consumer group tested hotel booking messages.
Britain's Competition and Markets Authority had pushed booking sites to be clearer.
The group found about half of the only one room left messages on one big site gave a misleading picture.
Online stores add countdowns, low stock bars and limited editions.
Sometimes the shortage is real, but often it is a nudge.
Wait one day, and see if the item returns.
Set a price alert, and let the store come to you.
Ask if you would want it at all without the warning.
Real bargains can wait for a calm mind.
Follow so you never miss the next trick, because we are not running out.

caption.en: Only two left! Scarcity makes things feel more valuable, and a famous cookie jar study shows why, with ways to stay calm when you shop.

en.text: Some money spent on gifts may be wasted.
In nineteen ninety three, economist Joel Waldfogel decided to measure it.
He surveyed students about gifts they got at Christmas.
They said they valued the gifts at about eighty four cents for every dollar spent.
That means a gap between what givers pay and what receivers value.
Later studies disagreed on the size, and some found little gap at all.
But the idea still helps you think before you buy.
Malls turn on lights, music and sales to make buying feel like love.
Deadlines like last day for delivery add a little panic.
Panic makes people pay more, think less, and buy things nobody needed.
Start with a budget, then divide it by the names on your list.
Ask people for a wish list, or ask what they actually need.
A gift card is often better than a guess.
Remember that time and attention are gifts too, and they cost nothing.
Spend well on the people, not on the pressure.
Follow for more holiday tricks before the next shopping rush.

caption.en: Why holiday gifts and sales can make us overspend, and what economists found when they asked whether Christmas gifts are worth what we pay.

en.text: Once, nothing in the shop had a price.
You walked in and the seller looked you over.
A rich looking customer might hear a higher price.
A poor looking one might get a lower one.
In eighteen sixty one, John Wanamaker opened Oak Hall in Philadelphia.
He is often credited with spreading a new idea: put the price right on the goods.
His motto was one price, and goods returnable.
He was not the only merchant to try fixed prices.
But department stores helped make it normal.
Fixed prices meant everyone walking in paid the same price.
That made shopping faster, and fairer for people who hated haggling.
Today your phone can show you the same item in ten different stores.
But the tag still has a few tricks left in it.
The number printed on it is only the start of the story.
Check what is included, what is extra, and what it costs per use.
A price tag is information, not a verdict.
Follow for more money history that explains your wallet today.

caption.en: Before price tags, shoppers haggled over everything, so here is the story of how fixed prices changed shopping forever.

en.text: The easiest button on your phone is the costliest.
Online shopping used to need forms, long steps and a lot of typing.
Every step gave you a little time to think twice about it.
In nineteen ninety seven, Amazon filed a patent for one click ordering.
It was granted in nineteen ninety nine.
Apple licensed the idea in two thousand.
The patent expired in twenty seventeen, and now buy now buttons are everywhere.
Why does it work? Paying hurts a little, and friction makes the hurt feel real.
Researchers call this the pain of paying.
Remove the steps and the pain disappears before you notice.
You are left holding the item, and later the bill.
To beat it, turn off one click ordering if you can.
Put things in your cart, and leave them there overnight.
In the morning, ask yourself whether you still really want it.
If you do, it will still be there.
A single night is the cheapest brake you will ever own.
Follow to learn which other buttons are built to hurry you.

caption.en: One click buying removes the pause where you might change your mind, so here is the patent story and how to put friction back.

en.text: Your menu was designed before you ever sat down.
Restaurants study which dishes make money and which only look good.
Then they arrange the menu to steer you.
In a Cornell University study, diners got menus with prices written three ways.
With dollar signs, with numbers only, or spelled out in words.
The numbers only menu got the highest spending.
Researchers think the dollar sign may remind you that you are paying.
Another study looked at where dishes sit in a list.
Items at the beginning or end of a category were up to twice as popular as those in the middle.
So the dish in the middle may be the one you never see.
Menus also use boxes, photos and flowery names to pull your eyes.
None of that is illegal, and some of it is just good design.
Read the whole menu, middle included.
Pick what you want first, then look at the price.
Ask yourself if you would order it without the fancy words.
Once you see the design, it loses its grip.
Follow for more secrets from behind the menu.

caption.en: Restaurant menus are designed to guide your order, with tricks like dollar signs, boxes and positions, and here is how to read them.

en.text: Picking your seat is a business of its own.
You find a flight for ninety nine dollars.
Then the seat map shows little squares with prices on them.
Choose a seat, and the flight suddenly gets more expensive.
Airlines call this unbundling: sell the flight cheap, then charge for every extra.
Families have felt it most.
A twenty twenty four law told the Department of Transportation to ban fees for seating young children beside a parent.
The rule was proposed that August, but check its status before you fly.
The fee works because you fear a middle seat and a bad trip.
That fear is the real product being sold to you.
Seats are often assigned free at check in.
Check in as early as you can, because the best free seats go first.
Compare the total price with the fee included, then decide.
Sometimes a pricier fare with the seat included is actually the cheaper choice.
Do the math before you click yes, and keep the saved money.
Follow for more travel tricks before you book your next flight.

caption.en: Airlines charge to choose your seat, and here is why basic fares leave you stuck, what the family seating rules say, and how to skip the fee.

category: Cards debt and buy now pay later

en.text: A small credit card balance can grow while you sleep.
Most cards charge interest every single day.
It is added to your balance, then tomorrow you pay interest on that too.
The Federal Reserve reported that accounts charged interest averaged about twenty two percent in twenty twenty five.
That is far more than most savings accounts pay you.
Now picture a thousand dollars left unpaid.
Pay only the minimum, and the balance barely moves for months.
The minimum payment is set to feel easy.
A federal law from two thousand nine made cards print how long minimum payments would take.
Look for that line on your statement.
It is usually much longer than people expect.
Pay the full statement balance every month if you can.
If you cannot, put extra money toward the card with the highest rate.
Set up automatic payments so you never pay a late fee on top.
Small extra payments shrink the snowball fast.
Interest works for banks, unless you make it work for you.
Follow for more ways to keep the math on your side.

caption.en: Credit card interest grows quietly every day, so here is how it works, what average rates look like and how to stop it from snowballing.

en.text: Your streaming bill keeps rising, quietly.
In January twenty twenty five, Netflix raised its standard plan in the United States.
It went from fifteen dollars and forty nine cents to seventeen dollars and ninety nine cents.
That is a bump of two dollars and fifty cents every single month.
Over a year, it adds thirty dollars.
Most people just keep paying, because switching feels like work.
That is the point of a small increase.
It is too small to feel, while cancelling takes time and effort.
Services also push you toward bundles and annual plans.
Meanwhile, you may have signed up for five of them over the years.
Make a list of every service and its monthly price.
Keep one or two at a time, and rotate each month.
Set a reminder to cancel the day after a show ends.
Cheaper plans with ads can cut the cost, if you can live with the breaks.
You can still watch everything you love, just not all at the same time.
Follow for more ways to take back your monthly bills.

caption.en: Streaming prices keep going up, so here is how small monthly increases add up and how to keep your entertainment budget under control.

en.text: Losing money hurts more than finding it feels good.
Psychologists call it loss aversion.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky made the idea famous, and Kahneman later won a Nobel Prize.
In a study from nineteen ninety, researchers gave some students a coffee mug.
They asked the mug owners what price they would sell it for.
Students without a mug were asked what they would be willing to pay.
Sellers asked for about seven dollars, more than twice as much.
Buyers offered about three.
Owning the mug, even for a few minutes, made giving it up feel like a loss.
Stores know this, and use it on purpose.
Free trials and money back offers let you own something first.
Giving it back then feels like losing something that was already yours.
Ask yourself if you would buy it today, at this price.
Treat every free trial as a test with a hard end date.
Set the cancel reminder the moment you sign up.
Notice the feeling, name it, and let your head make the final call.
Follow for more mind tricks that cost people money.

caption.en: Losing hurts more than winning feels good, a bias called loss aversion, so here is how a famous coffee mug experiment shows it and how to use it.

en.text: Compare at is not the same as was.
You see a jacket for fifty dollars and compare at one hundred and twenty.
It feels like a steal.
But compare at to what, and where?
The Federal Trade Commission warns that a comparison price must be honest.
California also requires that a former price was the prevailing price in the last three months.
Rules like these exist because of games played with price tags.
Shoppers often assume outlets sell leftovers from the main store.
Some items are made only for outlets, in different quality.
Either way, compare at invites you to feel smart.
Search the exact product name and model number online.
Use a price history tool, and see what it really sold for in recent months.
Judge by quality and need, not by the crossed out number on the tag.
The only discount that matters is against what you would have paid.
Is this worth the money I will actually hand over today?
Follow for more tag tricks and how to read them like a pro.

caption.en: The compare at price on the tag may not be what anyone paid, so here is how to read it and how to find the real price.

en.text: Casino carpets are loud on purpose, designers say.
It is bright, busy, and wild.
The carpet is not there for you to admire.
Some casino designers say loud patterns keep your eyes up on the machines, not down on the floor.
They also hide spills and wear in a place with heavy foot traffic.
There is little hard research on any of that, so treat it as design theory.
But the idea fits a much bigger pattern in how casinos are built.
Casino floors are often laid out as a maze of machines, with few straight lines.
Writer Natasha Dow Schull spent years studying gamblers and machines.
Her book, Addiction by Design, came out in twenty twelve.
It describes how the whole space and the machines can pull people into a rhythm.
Hours pass quietly, and the money goes with them.
Decide your budget and your time before you go in.
Take only that cash, and nothing else.
Leave when either one runs out, no exceptions.
Never chase a loss, because the house edge does not care.
Follow for more on how places are built to keep you inside.

caption.en: Casino carpets are loud and wild for a reason, and here is the design idea behind them and how to protect your money inside a casino.

category: Money habits that beat the tricks

en.text: The best money tool costs nothing.
You walk in for milk and bread.
You walk out with a full cart.
How did that happen?
A twenty twenty study found that wandering glances led to more unplanned purchases in the cart.
The researcher suggested a shopping list to keep attention on target.
Estimates of unplanned buying vary a lot, depending on how researchers count it.
But stores plan for it anyway.
Displays, free samples and big signs all pull your eyes away from the plan.
A good list starts at home, in your kitchen.
Check the fridge and the cupboards first, then write what you really need.
Put a rough price next to each item, and add them up before you go.
Eat before you go, because hunger makes everything on the shelf look good.
Use your phone for the list, and stick to the aisles you need.
Leave one small treat line, so that you do not feel punished.
A list turns a giant store into a short, easy walk.
Follow for more grocery habits that keep money in your pocket.

caption.en: A shopping list protects you from impulse buys, so here is the research on wandering eyes and how to build a list that works.

en.text: Even experts are fooled by the first price they see.
In nineteen eighty seven, two researchers tested real estate agents.
Each agent toured the same house and got the same facts.
Only one thing changed: the asking price on the listing.
Agents who saw a higher asking price valued the house at thousands of dollars more.
Agents who saw a lower one valued it lower.
Afterward, the agents said the asking price had not influenced them.
It had, and by a lot.
Car lots, furniture stores and online shops all start with a big first number.
The discount that follows feels like a gift.
But the gift was measured from a number they chose.
Before you shop, write down what you think a fair price is.
Look at three sold prices, not three asking prices.
For big buys, get a quote from a place that is not selling to you.
Be ready to walk away from a number you did not choose.
The price you pay should come from your head and your budget.
Follow to see through more of the numbers thrown at you.

caption.en: The first price you see can quietly change what you think is fair, even for experts, so here is the real estate study and how to resist it.

en.text: End of aisle displays are not always deals.
Piles of soda, chips and cereal stacked into a tower.
Prices on those towers are sometimes the same as on the regular shelf.
It looks like a sale.
Sometimes it is, but sometimes it is only a display.
Food companies can pay for prime spots, and stores can accept.
Retail research has long shown that displays and signs lift sales.
One common finding is that shoppers read a display as proof of a discount.
Sometimes even when the price did not move.
You see a stack and your brain says everyone else is buying it.
It is a shortcut that saves you from comparing.
The shelf tag tells you the actual price per unit, and a display often hides it.
Stores love when you skip comparing.
Treat an end display as a suggestion.
Check the price per ounce, and compare it with the regular shelf.
Look at the shelf label, not the big sign.
Remember that a pile is not a promise of a low price.
Buy it only if it was already on your list.
A display is just a billboard made of food.
Follow for more ways to read a store like a map.

caption.en: The big display at the end of the aisle is not always a bargain, so here is why stores put products there and how to check the real price.

en.text: You copy other people more than you think.
Imagine a card in a hotel bathroom asking you to reuse your towel.
In a famous study, researchers changed the words on that card.
One card talked about the environment.
Another said most guests in this room reuse their towels.
The room based message beat the usual environmental appeal.
People follow what similar people did in a similar place.
Retailers know that a crowd makes a choice feel safe and low risk.
Online stores use the same trick with stars, reviews and best seller badges.
Thousands of people liked this, so you might too.
A badge tells you what is popular, not what is good for you.
The crowd can be wrong, and it can also be bought.
Read the three star reviews first, because they are usually the most honest.
Ask what the product does for you, not for everyone.
Check the price against what you actually need.
If most people buy it, ask whether most people have your needs.
Popular is a fact about other people.
Your budget belongs to you alone.
Follow for more tricks that use the crowd against you.

caption.en: When other people do it, you feel safer doing it too, so here is the hotel towel study and how social proof is used to sell you things.

en.text: Gift cards in your drawer are free money left behind.
A Bankrate survey in twenty twenty four asked Americans about them.
About forty three percent said they had at least one unused gift card, voucher or store credit.
The average unused amount was two hundred and forty four dollars.
And about a third said they had lost money on a gift card.
Twenty percent let one expire, and seventeen percent lost one.
Why does it happen? A gift card feels like play money.
Some cards are never used, and that money stays with the store.
You spend a little more than the card, which is good for the store.
Put a note on your phone with the store and the balance.
Take a photo of the card, front and back.
Look for expiration dates, and use older cards first.
Use cards for things you already buy, like groceries.
Do not spend extra just to use up the balance.
Check whether the store has an online balance tool.
Can you sell or swap it for cash? Check first.
Even a partial value beats nothing.
Follow for more tricks to stop leaving money on the table.

caption.en: Millions of Americans leave gift cards unused, so here is what a Bankrate survey found and how to use every dollar.

en.text: The first credit card was almost a mistake.
In nineteen fifty, Diners Club launched in New York.
About two hundred people got the card, good in fourteen restaurants.
The famous story says the founder forgot his wallet at dinner.
That story may be a legend, but the card was real.
Then in September nineteen fifty eight, Bank of America mailed sixty thousand cards to people in Fresno.
Nobody had asked for them.
Each person got instant credit of a few hundred dollars.
It was chaotic, and the program lost twenty million dollars in its first year.
The idea was that merchants would take cards, and banks would take a fee.
But the idea stuck, and credit cards became part of daily life.
Plastic changed how we feel about spending.
You no longer hand over cash that you can count.
Instead you sign for a bill that arrives later.
A card is a great tool when you pay it off every month.
It becomes a trap when you do not.
Treat it like cash, because the bill comes either way.
Follow for more money history that explains your wallet.

caption.en: The first credit card was made of paper and mailed to strangers, and here is how Diners Club and the Fresno drop changed money forever.

en.text: Your saved card is making spending too easy.
Remember the last time you bought something online?
You did not type a number, because the site already had it.
That small change removes a pause.
Researchers call paying a pain, and friction is what makes you feel it.
Without friction, the pain disappears, and so does your hesitation.
There is a safety side as well.
Under federal law, your liability for stolen credit card charges is limited to fifty dollars.
Debit cards can be different, because the money leaves your account right away.
Rules for debit cards depend on how fast you report a problem.
Use a credit card for online shopping, not a debit card.
Turn off saved cards on sites you do not use much.
Use a unique password and turn on two step login.
Check your statements every month for charges you do not know.
A tiny pause before paying is a good thing.
It gives you time to ask if you really want it.
Follow for more everyday ways to protect your money.

caption.en: Saved cards make paying feel painless, so here is why that costs you and how to keep your card safe online with simple settings.

title.en: Do you read a menu like a book

en.text: You do not read a menu like a book.
It feels like you start at the top and work down.
But your eyes jump around.
In twenty eleven, two researchers tested menu positions.
Dishes at the start or end of a category were up to twice as popular as those in the middle.
Your brain remembers the first and the last best.
That is why the middle of a list can hide good value.
So restaurants may put the dishes they want to sell at the edges.
Servers add their own nudges, like today's special.
Prices at the end of a line can hide how much it all adds up.
A special sounds exclusive, but it can be the dish they want to sell.
Scan the whole menu before you start to decide.
Look at the middle on purpose.
Ask what is good value, and what the kitchen is proud of.
Then pick based on what you want, not where it sits.
A menu is a map made to move your eyes.
Follow for more ways to take back control of your order.

caption.en: People think they read a menu from top to bottom, but research says the edges matter most, so here is how that changes what you order.

en.text: That cheap flight price can be a trap.
You search for flights and see two prices.
One is cheap, and the other costs a bit more.
Delta started testing basic economy in twenty twelve.
You could not pick your seat in advance, and you could not make changes.
If you want a seat with your family, the cost can jump.
Other airlines followed with similar fares.
Some airlines even charge for a carry on bag on those fares.
Airlines use the cheap fare to win the search results.
Rules differ by airline and change over time, so read the fare details.
The low price gets you in, and the rules push you up.
Add a seat fee, a bag fee and a change fee.
Suddenly the cheap fare costs more than the regular one.
And you cannot change the ticket if your plans move.
Before you book, add up the total for your trip.
Do you need a bag, a seat or the option to change dates?
Compare the final price, not the first one.
If your plans are certain, basic can be fine.
If they are not, the flexible fare is insurance.
Follow for more travel math before you click book.

caption.en: Basic economy fares look cheap but remove seat choice and flexibility, so here is how to compare the real cost before you book.

category: Cards debt and buy now pay later

en.text: Zero percent can cost a lot of money.
You see a sofa with no interest for twelve months.
It sounds like free money.
And the store may have a financing partner that benefits from late payments.
But some offers use deferred interest.
Pay it off on time, and you pay no interest.
Miss the deadline by a day, and interest is charged back to the first day.
Not on what is left, but on the whole original amount.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau studied this in a twenty fifteen report.
It found most people paid in time, but those who missed often had most of the balance left.
Another government report counted about one billion dollars in deferred interest on medical financing.
The offer works because people think they will pay it off.
Ask one question: is this zero percent interest, or deferred interest?
If it is deferred, split the price by the months and set a reminder.
Aim to finish a month early.
A true zero percent offer does not charge back interest.
Follow for more fine print explained in plain words.

caption.en: A zero percent offer can hide deferred interest that comes back with a bite, so here is how to tell the safe kind from the risky one.

en.text: You probably pay for more things than you think.
A twenty twenty two survey of a thousand Americans asked about subscriptions.
People guessed they spent about eighty six dollars a month.
When they listed every one, the average was two hundred and nineteen.
That is a gap of a hundred and thirty three dollars.
And forty two percent said they paid for something they no longer used.
Why does it happen? Each charge is small and easy to forget.
Free trials turn into paid plans, and prices drift up.
Companies count on you forgetting, because inertia is a powerful force.
You sign up once, and the charge repeats forever.
Open your bank statement and find every recurring charge.
Look at your credit card statement too, because charges hide in both.
Write each one down with its monthly price.
Cancel what you did not use last month.
Ask yourself whether you would sign up for it today.
Send that money straight into your savings.
Do this audit again every three months.
Small leaks sink big boats.
Follow for more ways to stop the quiet leaks in your budget.

caption.en: Subscriptions pile up quietly, and a survey found people underestimate their monthly costs by about a hundred and thirty dollars, so here is how to audit yours.

en.text: Your brain treats the same dollar differently.
Economist Richard Thaler named it mental accounting.
Here is the experiment that shows it.
You bought a ten dollar ticket for a play, and lost it.
Would you buy another ticket?
Only forty six percent said yes.
Now picture this: you are about to buy the ticket, and you lose a ten dollar bill instead.
Eighty eight percent said they would still buy the ticket.
The money lost is exactly the same.
But a lost ticket goes into the entertainment bucket.
And cash feels like it belongs to no bucket at all.
Stores know this, and call a refund store credit or a bonus.
The label changes how the money feels, but the value stays the same.
A tax refund feels like free money, so it gets spent differently.
Treat every dollar as the same dollar.
Give big windfalls a job before you spend them.
A bonus can go half to savings and half to fun.
Decide the job of money before it lands.
Follow for more money tricks happening inside your own head.

caption.en: Your brain sorts money into mental buckets that do not follow logic, so here is the lost ticket experiment and how to spend smarter.

en.text: A bargain you do not need is not a bargain.
You find a coat for forty percent of the original price.
It feels like winning.
That feeling is the thrill of a deal.
But your closet already has three coats.
Stores mark things down in steps to clear space for new stock.
Each step makes the bargain look bigger.
And the fear of missing out gets louder.
Many clearance items are final sale, with no returns.
Sizes can be odd, and stock may be damaged or last season.
So the price is only one part of the cost.
Ask whether you would buy it at full price.
Write down the last time you wore something like this.
Divide the price by how many times you will use it.
A one hundred dollar coat worn fifty times costs two dollars a wear.
A cheap thing worn once is expensive.
Cheap but unused is the most expensive kind of cheap.
Try it on, check the seams, and read the return policy.
If you hesitate, you already know the answer.
Follow for more ways to enjoy sales without the regret.

caption.en: Clearance racks look like pure bargains, but a deal is only a deal if you needed it, so here is how to shop them without regret.

en.text: The free drink is the costliest one in the casino.
A waitress walks by and offers you a drink.
It is free, and it is polite.
The staff are friendly, and the glass keeps you at the table.
In twenty nineteen, researchers in Canada tested alcohol and gambling.
People played a roulette game after a drink or a placebo.
Those who drank bet more after losses than after wins.
Scientists call that chasing losses.
Meanwhile the cash machine in the corner makes it easy to keep playing.
It was one lab study, and results from other studies are mixed.
Still, it fits a pattern: slower judgment, bigger bets.
Casinos also know a free gift makes people feel they owe something back.
Psychologists call it reciprocity.
Decide how much you can lose before you walk in.
Skip the free drinks, or sip water instead.
Water costs nothing and keeps your head clear.
If you do drink, lower the limit, not raise it.
The goal is to leave with your plan, not your regret.
Follow for more ways to see the system and stay in charge.

caption.en: Free drinks at the casino tables are not really free, and a study on alcohol and betting shows why, so here is how to protect your money.

category: Money habits that beat the tricks

en.text: Bigger does not always mean cheaper.
You see a large jar and a small jar of the same sauce.
Bigger must be cheaper per ounce, right?
Bulk sounds smart and sometimes it is.
Britain's Competition and Markets Authority found bigger packs usually have a lower unit price, but not always.
Consumer Reports once found a store label that understated the price per pound.
Sales on small sizes can also beat the large ones.
Packages can shrink in size while the price stays the same.
Why does it work? Bigger looks like a better deal.
Brands count on that feeling.
The unit price is the cost per ounce, pound or sheet.
Look at the small number on the shelf tag.
If it is missing, use your phone.
Compare in the same unit, like ounces to ounces.
Divide the price by the amount, then compare.
Do it for items you buy often.
Bulk also fails if the food goes bad before you eat it.
Over a year, it adds up.
Five seconds of math can beat a coupon.
Follow for more tiny habits that quietly save big.

caption.en: The biggest package is not always the best deal, so here is how to use the unit price on the shelf tag to find the real bargain.

en.text: A store once tried to end sales, and it backfired.
In twenty twelve, J C Penney hired a new boss, Ron Johnson.
He wanted to drop coupons and constant sales.
It sounded fair, clean and modern.
Instead, he wanted everyday low prices that were fair and square.
It sounded honest and simple.
Many customers loved a sale more than the lower price itself.
The company's sales fell about twenty five percent that year.
It lost nearly a billion dollars.
Johnson was out after about sixteen months, and sales returned.
Shoppers did not want lower prices only.
They wanted a story: I found a deal.
They wanted the feeling of beating the price.
That feeling is a product the store sells too.
Know the real price before you shop.
Track the price for a few weeks, and look at the low.
Use a price history tool for big items.
Buy when your price is hit, not when the sign shouts.
The smartest shopper enjoys the game without playing it.
Follow to learn which prices are honest and which are theater.

caption.en: A famous store tried to end sales, and customers walked away, so here is what J C Penney learned about the was and now price game.

en.text: Those flowers by the door are doing a job.
You walk in, and you smell and see fresh color.
Why do stores greet you with flowers and fruit?
It is a design choice, not an accident.
Retail researcher Paco Underhill named the entrance zone the decompression zone.
His idea, from the book Why We Buy, is that shoppers take in little just after entering.
You are adjusting from the street.
Retail designers say stores use that moment to set a mood of freshness.
Fresh produce first makes the whole store feel fresh.
Then comes the bakery, the meat, and the snacks.
And it makes a cart feel healthy before the snacks.
After a few apples, a treat feels fair.
Some shoppers then feel they earned a treat.
Make your list before you step through the door.
Walk the edges, then shop the aisles on your list.
Stores put basic items at the back, so you pass many tempting products.
Buy flowers if you love them, not because the store told you to.
Noticing the design takes away its power.
Follow for more secrets from the doorway to the checkout.

caption.en: The flowers by the supermarket door are doing a job, and here is the shopping science of the entrance and how to stay on budget.

en.text: Doctors once appeared in ads for cigarettes.
In nineteen forty six, Camel launched a famous slogan.
The ads ran across magazines and radio for years.
More doctors smoke Camels than any other cigarette.
The ads claimed a survey of over one hundred thousand doctors backed it up.
Who could argue with a doctor?
Ads also used dentists, nurses and even athletes.
That is the authority effect: we trust people in white coats.
Today, the Federal Trade Commission has rules for endorsements.
That rule is about honesty, not about who looks smart.
An endorser must reflect honest opinions, and experts must really have the expertise they claim.
Still, health ads online keep using the same look.
A person in a lab coat, a chart, and a big claim.
The look sells before the proof does.
Ask who paid for the claim.
Look for a study you can find, not just a quote.
If a product says it cures everything, it probably cures nothing.
Real medicine shows its limits and its risks.
Talk to your own doctor before you spend.
Follow for more stories where trust was used as a sales tool.

caption.en: Ads once used doctors to sell cigarettes, so here is the true story of the Camel campaign and how to spot health claims that sound too good.

en.text: The week after Christmas is a huge return week.
People line up with boxes, bags and receipts.
Some gifts are returned because they are the wrong size or color.
The National Retail Federation expected returns in twenty twenty five to reach nearly eight hundred and fifty billion dollars.
It said retailers expect about seventeen percent of holiday sales to come back.
That is a lot of unwanted stuff.
Stores know returns cost money, so policies are getting tougher.
Some shorten the window, charge restocking fees, or require original packaging.
Some online returns cost shipping.
Read the return policy at the time you buy.
Take a photo of the receipt, and keep the box.
Many stores extend the holiday return window, but not all do.
Ask for a gift receipt, so the person can exchange it.
Honest gifts include a way out.
Return fast, before the window closes.
If you keep a gift, use it, and do not let it sit.
A good return turns a mistake into money again.
Follow for more tips to keep more of your holiday money.

caption.en: Returns after Christmas are big business, so here is what the National Retail Federation says about them and how to return or exchange smart.

en.text: The first coupon was a ticket for a free soda.
In the late eighteen eighties, Asa Candler took over Coca-Cola.
He had salesmen hand out tickets for one free glass.
Customers went to the fountain, and tried it for free.
The company later said it handed out millions of those tickets.
A free taste gave people a reason to try something new.
One estimate says about one in nine Americans got a free Coke this way.
Millions of tickets went out, and the habit grew.
Soon other brands copied the idea with mailed and printed coupons.
Today coupons live in apps, emails and codes.
They work, but they also steer your choice.
A coupon can make you buy a brand you did not want.
Check the expiration date before you plan around it.
Only use coupons for things on your list.
Compare the coupon price with the store brand.
If the coupon makes you spend more, skip it.
A discount on something you did not need is a loss.
A coupon should save money, not create a purchase.
Follow for more history behind the deals in your pocket.

caption.en: The first coupon was a handwritten ticket for a free soda, and here is how Coca-Cola used it to build a giant brand.

en.text: Someone just bought this, or maybe nobody did.
You are looking at a jacket online.
A box pops up: ninety seven other people are looking at this.
It feels like a race.
In twenty nineteen, researchers from Princeton and the University of Chicago studied about eleven thousand shopping sites.
They found one thousand eight hundred and eighteen examples of what they called dark patterns.
Those were on about eleven percent of the sites.
These tools can make a shop feel busy when it is quiet.
The team found some activity messages used random numbers, not real data.
The team also found companies that sell these tricks as ready made tools.
Not every message is fake, but you cannot tell from the screen.
Treat urgency messages like noise.
Ask whether the message is a fact or a feeling.
Close the tab, and come back tomorrow.
Real deals survive a night of sleep.
If the item is gone, another one will appear.
And it will often be cheaper.
Time is the strongest tool you have.
Follow for more online tricks and how to see through them.

caption.en: Someone just bought this may be a trick to rush you, so here is what a study of eleven thousand shopping sites found about fake urgency.

en.text: A dish nobody orders can sell another dish.
Imagine a menu with two pasta dishes, one cheap and one fancy.
Many people pick the cheap one, because the fancy one feels like too much.
Now add a third dish, priced just under the fancy one but clearly worse.
Hardly anyone orders it, and that is exactly the point.
Next to it, the fancy dish suddenly looks like a bargain.
In nineteen eighty two, three researchers named Huber, Payne and Puto tested this idea.
They showed that adding a worse choice can push people toward the better one next to it.
It works with cars, phone plans, hotel rooms and subscription tiers.
Look at any pricing page with three plans.
Later research found the effect is real, but not always strong.
Even so, businesses keep using it, because it is cheap and often works.
Ask which option you would pick if the decoy did not exist.
Compare the two real choices by what you need, not how they sit.
If the middle option looks too good, find out who it is helping.
A good deal still looks good with the decoy removed.
Follow for more menu and pricing tricks, explained in plain language.

caption.en: A decoy option nobody wants can make another option look like a bargain, and here is the research behind the decoy effect and how to resist it.

en.text: You used to get your first bag free.
Then in May two thousand eight, American Airlines announced a fifteen dollar fee for a first checked bag.
It was the first major airline to charge for it.
Other airlines followed within months.
Soon bag fees became normal across the industry, not a special case.
Today, bag fees are part of the business model.
The ticket looks cheap, then the bag makes it a regular fare.
Fees can also cost less online than at the airport counter.
Why do they work? You pay a small fee for each part, so the total feels hidden.
Researchers call it partitioned pricing.
Splitting a price into parts makes each part feel smaller than the whole.
Add the bag fee to the ticket before you compare airlines.
Pack in a single carry on if the rules allow it.
Pay for a bag online ahead of time, not at the gate.
Check if your airline card gives you a free bag.
The real price is the one with everything you need.
Follow for more tips to fly without the surprise charges.

caption.en: Baggage fees changed how airlines sell tickets, so here is how the first checked bag fee started in 2008 and how to pack smarter.

category: Cards debt and buy now pay later

en.text: Zero percent interest can still cost you money up front.
You get an offer in the mail to move your credit card debt for free.
Zero percent interest for more than a year sounds like a rescue.
Look closer, and you usually find a balance transfer fee.
It is often between three and five percent of the amount you move.
Move five thousand dollars with a three percent fee, and you pay one hundred and fifty dollars.
The fee is added to your balance on day one.
Then the clock starts on the promotional period.
When it ends, the rate jumps back to a normal, often higher, card rate.
And new purchases on the card may not get the same deal.
Divide the balance by the months of the offer.
That is the monthly payment that clears it on time.
If you cannot afford that payment, a transfer only delays the problem.
Do not use the card for anything else until it is paid.
A fee of one hundred and fifty dollars can still save you more than months of interest.
Follow for more card math that can save you real money.

caption.en: A zero percent balance transfer can still cost three to five percent up front, so here is how to run the numbers before you move debt.

en.text: Save twenty percent if you pay for the whole year.
It sounds smart, and sometimes it is.
But a year is a long time to forget something.
Many annual plans renew on their own, at the new price.
The notice may arrive in an email you never open.
In September twenty twenty five, Amazon agreed to pay two and a half billion dollars to settle a government case.
The agency said Prime customers were enrolled and kept in the program through confusing design.
Amazon did not admit wrongdoing.
The deal included one billion dollars in penalties and one and a half billion in refunds.
The case shows how subscription traps are built from small hurdles.
Before you pay for a year, ask if you will use it every month.
Set a reminder two weeks before renewal.
Use a virtual card or a card with an easy block.
Read the cancel rules before you hand over your card.
A discount is only a discount if you keep the thing.
Follow for more ways to cancel before they charge.

caption.en: Annual plans look cheaper but can lock you in or renew without warning, so here is what the FTC said about Amazon Prime and how to protect yourself.

en.text: The money you already spent should not decide anything.
You buy a ticket to a movie and it turns out to be terrible.
Do you stay for two hours because you paid?
In nineteen eighty five, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer tested this at Ohio University.
They sold season theater tickets at different prices, some of them discounted.
People who paid full price went to more plays in the first half of the season.
Why? They did not want to waste what they paid.
The cost was gone either way, but the pain of waste stayed.
The same pattern shows up in huge projects, like the Concorde jet.
The British and French governments kept funding it even as losses grew.
At home, it looks like a gym you hate, or a car that keeps breaking.
Ask this: if I had not spent anything yet, would I start today?
If the answer is no, stop.
The past money is gone, but the future money is still yours.
Cutting a loss can be the smartest save of all.
Follow for more ways to stop paying for a mistake twice.

caption.en: The sunk cost fallacy makes us keep spending because we already spent, so here is the theater ticket study and how to cut your losses.

en.text: A sale sign can sell things all by itself.
You see a red sign in a store window.
Your brain makes a quick guess: this must be cheaper.
Marketing researchers have found that sale labels can lift sales.
One study looked at a clothing catalog and found the effect weaker when many items had the label.
So a label works partly because it is rare.
Stores also use words like special, deal and last chance.
A word like deal makes you feel smart before you check anything.
These words are not always tied to a real price cut.
Always ask what the price was before the sign went up.
Online, banners shout sale in every corner of the page.
But a sale price is only good if it is below the usual price.
Look for the was price, and ask if it is honest.
Use a price tracker for anything above fifty dollars.
Know that many items go on sale on a regular cycle.
If you can wait, you often will see it again.
A sign is a message, not proof.
Follow for more signs, labels and prices decoded.

caption.en: A sale sign can raise sales all on its own, so here is how retailers use labels and what to check before you trust one.

en.text: Slot machines celebrate even when you lose.
You hear bells, chimes and a happy song.
It sounds like a win, so you assume it is one.
At the University of Waterloo, researcher Mike Dixon studied this.
In a twenty thirteen study, ninety six gamblers played with and without sound.
Some spins paid back less than the bet but still played celebration sounds.
Those are called losses disguised as wins.
With sound on, players overestimated how often they won, about twenty four percent compared with fifteen without it.
Skin tests also showed stronger arousal when the sounds played.
Most players said they preferred the sound.
Your ears reward you, even when your wallet does not.
That is the trap: it feels better, so you keep going.
Before you play, decide the most you will spend.
Mute the sound or wear earbuds with your own music.
Check your real balance, not how it feels.
Slot machines also show credits instead of dollars, which hides the real number.
When the money is gone, the music was never about you.
Follow for more on how casinos trick your ears and your head.

caption.en: Slot machines make winning sounds even when you lose money, and a University of Waterloo study shows how those sounds fool the ear.

category: Money habits that beat the tricks

en.text: Your inbox is a store that never closes.
Every day brings a new sale, a new code, a new deadline.
Each one is a small nudge to spend.
Marketers test subject lines to find the words that make people click.
Last chance, ends tonight, only a few hours left.
Those messages make you act before you think.
Fear of missing out beats good judgment, again and again.
The CAN-SPAM Act of two thousand three set rules for commercial email.
Senders must include a way to opt out, and honor it within ten business days.
Even so, unsubscribing yourself is still the surest fix.
Click unsubscribe at the bottom of emails from stores you know.
Do not click anything in a spam email that you do not recognize.
Make a second email address just for shopping.
Keep the main inbox for bills, friends and work.
Spend ten minutes a week cleaning the rest.
Then check which stores you shop at only because of emails.
You will see fewer deals, and you will spend less.
Silence is the cheapest discount you can get.
Follow for more habits that reclaim your attention and your money.

caption.en: Store emails push you to spend with urgency and offers, so here is how to unsubscribe safely and what the law says about it.

en.text: Why do luxury items often have round prices?
A bottle of champagne priced at one hundred dollars looks smooth.
A bottle at ninety eight dollars and seventy six cents looks odd.
In a study published in twenty fifteen, researchers Monica Wadhwa and Kuangjie Zhang tested this.
They found round prices felt right when a purchase was driven by feelings.
And non round prices felt right when a purchase was practical.
In one test, a camera for a family vacation was favored at a round price.
A camera for a class project was favored at a price with odd cents.
A later replication did not support the full effect, so treat it as an idea, not a law.
Still, stores use both styles for different moods.
A round price says treat yourself.
An odd price says this is a smart buy.
Notice which price style is being used on you.
Then ask what you actually want, not how the number sounds.
Prices speak to feelings, so listen with your head.
Follow for more tricks hidden inside ordinary numbers.

caption.en: Round prices feel right for treats and non round prices for practical buys, so here is what one study found and a caveat on later tests.

en.text: January first makes people feel like a new person.
It is the day of diets, gym cards and big money plans.
In twenty fourteen, researchers Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis named it the fresh start effect.
They looked at Google searches for diet, and found jumps after New Year.
They also found more gym visits at the start of a week, a month or a semester.
A new date feels like a clean page, with the old mistakes left behind.
Look at your bills, and pick the one you can cut first.
Retailers know that, and put diet, fitness and organizing sales on the calendar.
You may sign up before the motivation fades.
The effect is short, so plan for week three.
Use the fresh start for one money goal.
Pick a small, clear one, like saving twenty dollars a week.
Automate the transfer so that the plan does not need willpower.
Use other fresh starts, like your birthday or a Monday.
You do not need January to begin.
Follow for more small money habits that last past the first week.

caption.en: New Year and other fresh starts motivate us to change, and marketers know it, so here is the fresh start effect and how to use it for money.

en.text: The smell in a store is not an accident.
You walk in and smell fresh bread, vanilla or oranges.
It feels like home, and it makes you hungry.
Smell goes straight to the parts of the brain tied to memory and mood.
In a Swiss study in a home decoration shop, researchers tested scents over eighteen days.
One group of shoppers spent about twenty percent more when a simple scent filled the air.
It was one study, and results across stores vary.
The point is that smell works below your attention.
But retailers use scent, music and light to set a mood.
A bakery near the entrance can make the whole store feel warm.
You feel good, so you feel relaxed about spending.
A hungry shopper tends to buy more than planned.
Eat something before you go grocery shopping.
Stick to your list, even if the bread smells amazing.
Buy the bread, if you love it, and keep the rest as planned.
Noticing a trick is half the way to beating it.
Follow for more tricks hiding in plain sight.

caption.en: Stores use scent to shape your mood, and a Swiss shop study found a simple smell raised spending, so shop smart.

en.text: That recommendation from your favorite creator may be an ad.
They smile, hold up a product and say they love it.
It feels like a friend telling you a tip.
In April twenty seventeen, the Federal Trade Commission sent about ninety letters to influencers and brands.
It reminded them to clearly disclose paid relationships.
Brands pay influencers with money, products or free trips.
The agency pointed to its Endorsement Guides.
Why does it matter? We trust people more than ads.
A paid post works because it does not look like an ad.
The more real it feels, the more money it can make.
Discount codes and links are common signs of a deal.
That does not make the product bad.
Look for words like ad, sponsored or paid partnership.
Search for reviews from people with no link to the brand.
Compare the price with other options.
Check whether a cheaper version exists.
If you buy, buy because you need it.
Trust the facts more than the face.
Follow for more ways to see the sale behind the smile.

caption.en: Influencer posts can be paid ads, so here is what the FTC told influencers in 2017 and how to spot an ad in your feed.

en.text: Loyalty programs started with tiny pieces of paper.
In eighteen ninety six, Sperry and Hutchinson began offering stamps to retailers.
Shoppers got stamps with each purchase.
They pasted them in a book, and traded the book for goods.
By the nineteen sixties, stamps were everywhere.
The company said it printed more stamps than the Postal Service.
Why did it work? Collecting made shoppers feel they earned something.
It also brought them back to the same store.
A full stamp book felt like money you would waste if you left.
Today the stamps are apps, points and tiers.
The same idea sits behind store cards and miles.
The reward may be real, but so is the cost to earn it.
Ask how much you spend to get one dollar back.
That is the sunk cost trap in a loyalty card.
Join programs for stores you already shop at.
Do not buy extra to reach a point goal.
Check how long your points last.
A reward is a gift only if you wanted to buy anyway.
Follow for more history behind the rewards in your wallet.

caption.en: Loyalty programs started with paper stamps, so here is the story of S and H Green Stamps and how rewards still shape what you buy.

en.text: A shed once became the best restaurant in London.
In twenty seventeen, writer Oobah Butler made a listing for The Shed at Dulwich.
It was a real shed in his garden, not a restaurant.
He had friends post glowing reviews, and the listing climbed the ranks.
Within months, it was number one among London restaurants on the site.
Eventually he admitted the joke, and removed the listing.
Fake reviews are not just a prank.
In twenty thirteen, the New York attorney general reached settlements with nineteen companies over fake reviews.
They paid more than three hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
In twenty twenty four, the Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule banning fake reviews.
It allows penalties of over fifty thousand dollars per violation.
Read the three star reviews first.
Look for details, not just praise.
Real reviews mention small things, like a delay or a broken zipper.
Check if many reviews arrived on the same day.
Trust patterns, not stars.
A product with thousands of five star reviews and no complaints should worry you.
Five minutes of doubt can save fifty dollars.
Follow for more online tricks and how they get caught.

caption.en: Fake reviews can fool you, and a shed once became the top restaurant on TripAdvisor, so here is the story and how to spot fake praise.

title.en: The expensive dish as an anchor

en.text: The most expensive dish may not be there to sell.
You open a menu and see a steak for eighty dollars.
You would never order it.
The price makes the next dish feel like a reasonable decision.
But then the thirty dollar chicken looks like a deal.
That is anchoring: the first number sets your sense of normal.
In a famous experiment, a spinning wheel changed what people guessed.
A random number pulled their answers up or down.
Menu consultants teach restaurants to use the same effect.
Wine lists use it too, with a few very high bottles at the top.
The average bottle then looks fairly priced.
Decide how much you want to spend before you read the menu.
Ignore the top price when you judge the rest.
Compare dishes with each other on the same scale.
Ask what you would pay if the expensive dish was not there.
Order what fits your plan, not what feels cheap next to the anchor.
A menu is a story about price.
Follow to learn how to read the whole story, not just the top.

caption.en: An expensive dish on the menu makes the next dish look cheap, so here is how menu anchoring works and how to order for value.

en.text: Your gym membership may be a donation.
You sign up in January with big plans.
By March, you have been twice.
Economists Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier studied this in a famous paper.
They looked at three health clubs and thousands of members.
People on a monthly contract paid over seventy dollars a month.
That is more than eight hundred dollars a year, for a few visits.
They went about four times a month on average.
That works out to more than seventeen dollars a visit.
But the clubs also sold ten visit passes for ten dollars a visit.
The authors said people overestimate how often they will go.
On average, members lost around six hundred dollars over their membership.
Start with a pay per visit option or a short trial.
Count your real visits after one month, honestly.
Gyms also make it hard to cancel in some cases.
If you do not go, cancel the same day.
Divide the fee by your visits, and see what you pay.
Follow for more ways to stop paying for good intentions.

caption.en: Most gym memberships go unused, and a famous study found people paid more than they needed, so here is how to avoid wasted fees.

en.text: A longer flight can cost less than a shorter one.
You search for a flight to Chicago and see a high price.
Then you see a flight to a farther city, with a stop in Chicago, for less.
Some travelers book the farther flight and leave the trip at the stop.
It is called hidden city ticketing.
Airlines say it breaks their contract rules.
In twenty fourteen, United and Orbitz sued a man who ran a site for it.
The case was dismissed in twenty fifteen over jurisdiction.
In twenty nineteen, Lufthansa sued a passenger in Germany who skipped his last flight.
A Berlin court dismissed the case, saying the airline's terms were not clear enough.
This is not legal advice, but the practical risks are real.
Checked bags go to the final stop, so you must carry on.
If an early flight changes, the rest of your ticket may be cancelled.
Compare normal fares on several dates first.
Know the rules of your airline, and the risk to your miles.
Follow for more travel money tricks and the fine print behind them.

caption.en: Hidden city tickets can look cheaper but come with real risks, so here is what airlines say and what courts have decided.

category: Cards debt and buy now pay later

en.text: A higher credit limit is not a gift.
Your card company sends a message: good news, your limit just went up.
It feels like a reward for being responsible.
It also lifts your spending power.
You see room, and your brain wants to fill it.
Economists Jonathan Gross and Nicholas Souleles studied credit card account data.
They found that when limits rose, people borrowed more soon after.
About thirteen cents of each extra dollar of limit became new debt in a few months.
That means a one thousand dollar increase can lead to about one hundred and thirty dollars more debt.
The effect was strongest for people near their limit.
More debt means more interest for the bank.
You can say no to an increase.
Ask for a smaller limit if it helps you stay in control.
Many issuers let you set a lower limit in the app.
Use a spending cap that you set yourself.
A good limit is one you never need.
Your limit should serve your plan.
Follow for more card tricks that look like favors.

caption.en: A credit limit increase feels like a reward, but a famous study found people spend and borrow more, so here is what to know before you say yes.

en.text: Airline miles are money the airline can change.
You collect them for years, and then the rules shift.
Award prices go up, and your balance buys less.
In the mid twenty tens, the big airlines switched to rewarding miles by dollars spent.
In twenty twenty, United borrowed about six point eight billion dollars backed by its frequent flyer program.
Appraisals valued American's program at between nineteen and thirty one billion dollars.
These programs are worth huge sums, and analysts say sometimes more than the airline itself.
That is why they print miles like a currency.
Banks buy miles from airlines and hand them out for card spending.
The more miles in the world, the less each one can be worth.
Do not hoard miles for a someday trip.
Use them when you find a good deal.
Check the value per mile before you book.
Never pay interest on a card to earn miles.
Miles are worth most when they are fresh.
Follow for more on the rewards that are not as sweet as they look.

caption.en: Airline miles can lose value overnight because airlines control the rules, so here is how loyalty programs became worth billions and how to use miles smartly.

en.text: Your brain prefers a little now over more later.
Would you take fifty dollars today or sixty in a month?
Many people take the fifty.
Economist David Laibson wrote about this in nineteen ninety seven.
He showed that people discount the near future much harder than the far one.
Researchers also call this hyperbolic discounting.
We are patient when we plan, and impatient when the moment arrives.
Tomorrow's you looks like a stranger to today's you.
Stores and apps are built for the moment.
Buy now, pay later, and enjoy it tonight.
Your future self gets the bill.
The fix is to decide in advance, when you are patient.
Set up an automatic transfer to a savings account on payday.
Even twenty dollars a week adds up over a full year.
Make the future step the default one.
If you never see the money, you will never miss it.
Write down one goal, and give it a date on the calendar.
Your future self will thank you quietly.
Follow for more tricks to help the you of tomorrow.

caption.en: Present bias makes us choose now over later, and economists study why, so here is how to make your future self win with simple money habits.
